phonemes.desc: Voiceless velar stop [k], as in English 'keep'; Middle Welsh writes it with either c or k, and the manuscripts vary between Cei and Kei.
The falling diphthong [əi] — a neutral first element gliding to [i], exactly the sound of Modern Welsh ei as in 'Cai', and of the English name Kay.

pronunciation.approximation: 'KAY' — one syllable, exactly the English name Kay; the diphthong glides from a neutral 'uh' to 'ee' inside a single beat.

pronunciation.note: Kai is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: Middle Welsh writes the name in plain Latin letters, so there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The capital alone distinguishes the temple form from the input; the hero's standing in the tradition is beside the point.

domains.title: The Steward of Arthur's Hall
domains.subtitle: The Nine Days' Breath, the Fire in His Hands, and the Sword No Physician Can Heal
domains.lead: Cei son of Cynyr is the first companion Arthur assigns to Culhwch: the tall man of the Mabinogion's oldest Arthurian tale, who could hold his breath nine nights and nine days under water, go nine nights and nine days without sleep, deal a wound no physician could heal, grow as tall as the tallest tree in the forest, and carry so much heat in his body that rain dried a handbreadth above and below his hand and his companions lit their fires from him in the cold. Centuries of romance would remember him as the steward of the court — the seneschal Kay.

cards.name: The Nine Days' Breath
cards.desc: Nine nights and nine days under water; nine nights and nine days without sleep — the Mabinogion's measure of the tall man's endurance.

cards.name: The Fire in His Hands
cards.desc: His heat kept his hand dry a handbreadth in the hardest rain; in the bitterest cold he was fuel for his companions' fire.

cards.name: The Unhealable Sword
cards.desc: A wound from Cei's sword no physician could heal — and the sword of Wrnach the giant came into Arthur's hand by Cei's trickery.

cards.name: The Seneschal's Office
cards.desc: Geoffrey of Monmouth's Caius dapifer — steward of Arthur's household, given Anjou, buried at Chinon: the office the later romances never let him leave.

symbols.name: The nine days' breath
symbols.meaning: Endurance past the human limit — the hero who outlasts water and sleep alike

symbols.name: The fire in his hands
symbols.meaning: Heat as provision: the companion who keeps the whole company warm, dry, and fed with fire

symbols.name: The unhealable sword
symbols.meaning: A stroke beyond remedy — the oldest stratum's mark of the warrior, before romances made him a steward

symbols.name: The beard of Dillus
symbols.meaning: The quest accomplished by cunning — and Arthur's mocking englyn that ended the fellowship

symbols.name: Cei Hir, 'the Tall'
symbols.meaning: Tall as the tallest tree in the forest when it pleased him — stature as the visible sign of the older, larger hero

mythology.lead: Kai's mythology lives in the oldest stratum of Welsh Arthurian tradition: Culhwch ac Olwen gives him the tale's largest dossier after Arthur himself, and the fragmentary dialogue poem Pa Gur remembers exploits the prose never told. The later Latin and French traditions kept the man and quietly spent the magic.

myths.title: The First Companion
myths.text: When Culhwch comes to Arthur's court to win Olwen daughter of Ysbaddaden Chief Giant, Arthur grants him help, and the first companion named is Cei son of Cynyr. The warrior-list fixes his peculiarities in one breath: nine nights and nine days he could be under water; nine nights and nine days he could go without sleep; a wound from Cei's sword no physician could heal. Cei the Tall — when it pleased him he could make himself as tall as the tallest tree in the forest. And the list adds the attribute the whole fellowship depended on: when the rain was heaviest, whatever he carried in his hand stayed dry for a handbreadth above and below, so great was his heat; and when the cold was hardest on his companions, he was fuel to them to light their fire. The list also preserves his mother's prophecy that his heart would be cold — the oldest trace of the coldness the later romances turned to mockery.

myths.title: The Salmon and the Sword
myths.text: Two of the hardest anoethau — the 'things hard to get' that Ysbaddaden sets as the bride-price — fall to Cei. To free Mabon son of Modron from his prison at Caer Loyw, the company follows the oldest animals to the Salmon of Llyn Llyw, and Cei and Bedwyr ride up the Severn on the salmon's shoulders; while Arthur's men assault the fort from the front, Cei carries Mabon away on the salmon's back. And when Arthur's band comes to the hall of Wrnach the giant, whose sword is needed to hunt the boar Twrch Trwyth — no guest had ever left that hall alive — Cei claims to be a master polisher of swords. Admitted, he burnishes the giant's blade, asks to hold it to test the work, and strikes Wrnach's head off with his own sword; the company destroys the fortress. The wonder-hero's greatest feats in the tale are won with a craftsman's hands, not a charge of horse.

myths.title: The Beard of Dillus and the Englyn
myths.text: The beard of Dillus the Bearded was wanted to make a leash for the whelp Drudwyn, and Cei and Bedwyr found the giant alone. Cei dug a pit, tricked Dillus into it, plucked his beard out with wooden tweezers, and killed him afterward — and Arthur, watching, sang an englyn mocking Cei for making a leash from a living beard he could never have taken from a healthy man. Cei answered nothing, but the tale records the consequence in a line: because of that englyn there was enmity between Cei and Arthur ever after, and Cei took no part in the hunt of Twrch Trwyth. The tale's closing tally keeps the ending: Gwyddog son of Menestyr slew Cei, and Arthur slew Gwyddog and his brothers to avenge him — the rift repaired only in vengeance.

myths.title: Nine Witches and the Cat of Anglesey
myths.text: The fragmentary dialogue poem Pa Gur yv y Porthaur?, preserved in the Black Book of Carmarthen, shows Arthur and the gatekeeper Glewlwyd Mighty-grasp trading boasts, and the boasts are Cei's: Cei pierced nine witches, and Cei the Fair went to Anglesey to destroy the monster the Welsh called Cath Palug — the gigantic cat that the triads say was born of the sow Henwen and raised by the sons of Palug as one of the island's plagues. The poem breaks off in the middle of that account, and scholars read the torn ending as the oldest trace of Cei's own death-fight. The early verse remembers him where the prose does not: as the champion sent against the things no one else would face.

myths.title: Caius Dapifer
myths.text: Geoffrey of Monmouth, writing about 1136, Latinizes him as Caius dapifer — Kay the steward — and gives him the seneschal's office and the province of Anjou at Arthur's plenary court at Caerleon, while Bedwerus the cupbearer receives Normandy. In Geoffrey's Roman war Kay fights as duke, is mortally wounded in the great battle against Lucius, and dies; Geoffrey says he was buried at Chinon, the castle he himself had built, mourned by the whole army. The magic is gone — no nine days' breath, no fire in the hands — but the office Geoffrey fixed to the name proved more durable than any peculiarity: from this book onward, Kay is the steward of Arthur's court in every language that tells the story.

lore.syncretism: Kai is less a figure who absorbed other gods than one whom each retelling rewrote. The Welsh stratum gives a wonder-hero: the tall, fire-handed, sleepless companion whose attributes belong to the oldest legendary stock of Britain. Geoffrey of Monmouth euhemerizes him into Caius dapifer, a duke and steward of recognizable twelfth-century type; Chrétien de Troyes turns the steward's sharpness into Keu's venomous tongue, the court's mocker who is always wrong; and Malory resolves the long arc into Sir Kay, Arthur's foster-brother — loyal, loud, and forever outmatched. Scholars have long paired him with Bedwyr, his constant companion in Culhwch ac Olwen, as the two oldest members of Arthur's band; and Mac Cana and others note that the tale-patterns around the pair — the raid on a giant's stronghold, the hunt of the enchanted boar — have close Irish analogues, though no Irish cycle preserves Cei himself. The transformation of the tall man into the seneschal is the tradition's own syncretism: one name, four costumes, and the office outlasting the magic.
lore.culturalLegacy: The steward outlived the giant-killer. Malory's Sir Kay — the foster-brother who claims he drew the sword from the stone, confesses, and is made seneschal at Arthur's coronation — fixed the English image: blunt, envious, brave enough, and indispensable to the household. Chrétien's Keu had already made him the court's satirist, and the romances of every language kept that register. T. H. White's The Sword in the Stone made Kay the human counterweight to the Wart, the brother who gets the crown's shadow instead of the crown. In Welsh the name never left: Cai remains a living given name, and the Mabinogion's Cei Hir is still the tall man of the oldest Arthurian tale. Modern scholarship treats the arc from wonder-hero to comic steward as one of the great case-studies in how the Arthurian legend domesticated its oldest figures.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Kai is the patron of the unglamorous power: the one who keeps the fire, the stores, the hall — the office that lets everyone else be heroic. His oldest attributes are a steward's attributes written in mythic scale. He does not merely endure the cold; he is fuel for the company's fire. He does not merely keep dry; whatever he carries stays dry a handbreadth around. The seneschal of the romances is the same figure after the magic has been spent: the man who knows where everything is kept, who answers the gate, whose sharp tongue is the friction of service worn into habit.

And the tradition is honest about the cost. His mother's prophecy said his heart would be cold; Arthur's englyn mocked the feat no one else could perform; the fellowship ended in a vengeance taken too late. Kai asks the question every household and every court must answer: what do you owe the one who keeps the fire — and what does keeping it do to the heart?
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is attested in Middle Welsh manuscripts as Cei, with the spelling variants Kei and Kai — plain Latin letters in Insular script, c. 12th–14th c. CE, in the Black Book of Carmarthen, the White Book of Rhydderch, and the Red Book of Hergest. No diacritic and no distinctive letter is involved: the normalized form is already ASCII, and the restoration Kai differs from the input only by its capital. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: kai.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Kai is a literary figure: no inscription, ogham stone, or Romano-British dedication names him, and Welsh tradition generally left texts rather than cult monuments for its heroes. His manuscript witnesses are exact and early. The dialogue poem Pa Gur survives in the Black Book of Carmarthen (c. 1250), the oldest substantial manuscript of Welsh verse; Culhwch ac Olwen survives in a fragmentary copy in the White Book of Rhydderch (Peniarth 4–5, c. 1350) and complete in the Red Book of Hergest (Jesus College MS 111, c. 1375–1425); and the Otherworld-raid poem Preiddeu Annwn, the companion witness to this stratum, is preserved in the Book of Taliesin (Peniarth 2, early 14th c.). Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae (c. 1136) and Lifris of Llancarfan's Vita Cadoci (c. 1100) carry the Latin attestations. The places of the tales — Caer Loyw on the Severn, the Anglesey of Cath Palug — remain on the map, but the tall man himself left nothing in stone.
